title: Private VPC networking runtime deep dive
next_steps: Share Private VPC network diagram and PrivateLink config (Redwood)
Schedule bench: p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput (customer + SE)
Confirm allowed IP ranges and NAT design (customer)
Follow-up on PrivateLink pricing and egress considerations (Redwood)

summary: Redwood SE and AE walked Aurelius Systems through Private VPC networking options for private deployments: PrivateLink vs NAT egress, subnet design, DNS resolution, and implications for runtime performance (latency/throughput), KV cache locality, batching and quantization. Action items include sharing network diagram and SOC2 docs, scheduling benchmarks, and confirming IP allowlist.
topics: Latency impact on KV cache and batching
Quantization and model variants for private deployments
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-09-15 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Raman, Samir Kapoor (Redwood) -- Mark Voss, Lina Ortega, Tej Patel (Aurelius)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, uh we're going to run through private vpc networking options and how they map back to runtime perf concerns. Priya will lead most of the deep tech bits, I'll cover rollout/ops and pricing.
[00:12] Mark Voss: Great thanks Alex. Quick note, we have Lina from cloud security and Tej on infra. We're mainly evaluating private deployment to avoid any egress of PII, and we care about sub 50ms token latencies for our chat flows.
[00:28] Priya Raman: Cool, thanks Mark. Just to set expectations: we'll cover PrivateLink, nat/egress paths, subnet layouts, DNS resolution patterns, and then map to things like batching, kv cache locality, and quantization tradeoffs. Any constraints we should know up front?
[00:41] Lina Ortega: Our VPC is fairly locked down; we'll need SAML SSO to the control plane, and all outbound to Redwood must go via PrivateLink or a peered egress. No unmanaged internet egress for inference nodes.
[00:55] Tej Patel: Also: we have multiple AZs, and we'd prefer multi-AZ for redundancy. We want to understand cross-AZ traffic costs and latency.
[01:07] Priya Raman: Good. Quick high-level: PrivateLink gives you an AWS-managed endpoint that keeps traffic on the AWS network to Redwood's endpoint; client traffic never leaves the AWS backbone. NAT egress means the inference instances will use NAT Gateway to reach Redwood public endpoints — that has different security and egress cost implications.
[01:28] Alex Chen: And just to add, for Dedicated/Private deployments Redwood can be deployed as a control plane in our managed plane while you host runtime in your VPC; the control plane calls back over PrivateLink for management.
[01:41] Mark Voss: Okay, so question: for runtime traffic (model inference), will latency be materially different between PrivateLink and direct VPC-hosted runtime?
[01:53] Priya Raman: Short answer: PrivateLink is lower variance and avoids NAT traversal, so p99 is typically better. But if you're hosting the runtime in your VPC (on-prem/private tenancy) and the KV cache is local to the runtime, that's ideal. The key is cache locality: if KV cache lives across VPC boundaries you'll see added RTTs per token.
[02:12] Tej Patel: When you say per token RTTs, can you quantify? We're seeing 20ms baseline TPU hops, want to know realistic numbers.
[02:22] Priya Raman: Sure — rough ballpark from similar setups: local KV cache hit path (same subnet/AZ) adds ~1-3ms per token for memory/lookup and processing overhead; cross-AZ within same cloud can add 2-5ms; crossing NAT to a remote Redwood-managed cache could add 10-50ms depending on path and NAT respawn. If your workloads are short-turn chat (50 tokens), that delta compounds.
[02:46] Mark Voss: That's significant. So we should aim to co-locate cache in VPC or ensure KV cache is pinned to runtime nodes?
[02:55] Priya Raman: Exactly — for low latency you want KV cache local to the runtime. Redwood supports deploying both the runtime and cache within customer VPC in the Private deployment model, so lookups are local. If you must use a managed cache outside the VPC, prefer PrivateLink and a dedicated ENI at the endpoint to minimize NAT/translation steps.
[03:13] Lina Ortega: For PrivateLink we need to confirm security posture: are connections over interface VPC endpoints encrypted?
[03:19] Alex Chen: Yes — PrivateLink uses TLS over the AWS backbone; traffic doesn't traverse public internet. We'll also provide mTLS options for service-to-service auth and you can bring your own keys via KMS/HSM.
[03:29] Tej Patel: Can you walk us through subnet design? We currently use /20 for prod; we'd like separate subnets for runtime, management, and metrics.
[03:39] Priya Raman: Common pattern: dedicate private subnets per AZ for runtime worker nodes, a separate control-plane-facing subnet (or team uses PrivateLink endpoint subnets), and a management subnet for telemetry/metrics. Avoid colocating heavy egress NAT gateways in the runtime subnets to prevent hairpinning. Use route tables per subnet and explicit endpoints for S3, ECR if pulling images.
[04:01] Mark Voss: What about DNS? We have split-horizon DNS and internal domains. How does Redwood resolve service endpoints?
[04:08] Priya Raman: With PrivateLink we give you an interface endpoint DNS name in your VPC — you can map that to your internal names with conditional forwarding. For control plane callbacks we support customer-managed DNS entries; the runtime can be configured to use your internal resolvers. Note: ensure IP address capacity on the endpoint subnet because ENIs consume addresses.
[04:28] Tej Patel: Good call on ENI count. If we scale to 200 concurrent workers per AZ, what's the ENI / port density we should expect?
[04:36] Priya Raman: ENI growth depends on how you configure the endpoint. Typically expect a handful of ENIs per AZ per endpoint, but for very high connections we'll advise scaling endpoint subnets and use multiple endpoints. We'll share a sizing guide (see action items).
[04:49] Samir Kapoor: Quick interjection — on the runtime side we also optimize by pooling connections and using persistent keepalives, which reduces ephemeral connection churn to PrivateLink endpoints.
[05:00] Mark Voss: Let's talk about throughput and batching. We have bursty traffic but overall high qps for embedding pipelines. What patterns should we follow?
[05:10] Priya Raman: For throughput, batching helps a lot but is latency-constraint dependent. If your application tolerates a few 10s of ms, configure continuous batching with a max batch size tuned to model. Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching and latency SLO targets; you can configure target p50/p95. For Private VPC, ensure workers can both reach the model weights (EFS or local disk) and have low-latency KV cache to keep batch prep fast.
[05:35] Tej Patel: Quantization—if we run int8 or 4-bit quantized models, does that change network patterns?
[05:41] Priya Raman: Quantization mainly reduces memory footprint and inference CPU/GPU time; network patterns are mostly unchanged, but smaller model footprints speed cold starts and model transfer if you're pulling weights over the network. If you rely on on-demand scaleups, quantized models reduce warmup cost. For sustained high throughput, it's more about GPU utilization than network.
[06:02] Mark Voss: How does the KV cache impact batching? If a request needs cache misses that go to the store, does that block the batch?
[06:11] Priya Raman: Good question. Redwood's runtime accommodates asynchronous cache lookups; we try to hydrate cache before the heavy compute path. However, worst case a miss can add latency to a request in a batch if the batch is being assembled and waiting on lookups. That's why local, fast cache with sub-ms or low-ms lookups is recommended. Also you can configure a fallback policy to serve from a slower path but mark the token as approximate; depends on your quality tolerance.
[06:39] Lina Ortega: From a security perspective, does KV cache store PII? We'll need encryption at rest and strict ACLs.
[06:46] Alex Chen: Yes, you can encrypt cache at rest using your KMS keys and control access via IAM/SG rules. We also support token scrubbing and redaction policies in the pipeline before anything is persisted.
[06:57] Mark Voss: Are there any hidden egress costs with PrivateLink vs NAT?
[07:03] Priya Raman: PrivateLink reduces public NAT egress charges because traffic stays on the AWS backbone, but AWS charges an hourly + per-GB fee for interface endpoints. Compare that to NAT Gateway per-GB egress and per-hour costs. We'll produce a sample cost model for both options.
[07:18] Tej Patel: Ok. Can we do a short sketch of request flow for us: client -> runtime -> kv cache -> model -> return; include where PrivateLink sits.
[07:27] Priya Raman: Sure. (brief pause) Client in app VPC calls the runtime worker in same subnet; runtime checks local KV cache; on hit, it proceeds to model decode; if miss and cache is remote, it calls cache endpoint (PrivateLink) within VPC and hydrates; model step runs on local GPU; response returns. If runtime is in a different VPC, you'd have PrivateLink between VPCs for runtime-to-cache calls. In a Redwood-managed remote cache scenario, runtime calls Redwood's PrivateLink endpoint and that stays on the backbone.
[07:58] Mark Voss: For multi-AZ, do you recommend cache replication per AZ?
[08:04] Priya Raman: Yes, replicate or partition by AZ for lowest latency. Cross-AZ reads okay but add ms. For consistency you can use async replication or a coordination layer; depends on your correctness needs.
[08:15] Samir Kapoor: Strategy we've seen: colocate a small local LRU cache per worker for hot prefixes plus a regional shared cache for warm state. That minimizes cross-network hits.
[08:25] Mark Voss: Sounds good. Let's talk about monitoring and traces — we need token-level latency breakdowns.
[08:31] Priya Raman: Redwood Console exposes token-level timing (KV lookup, model time, batching wait). For Private deployments we emit those metrics to your CloudWatch/Prometheus via push gateway and you can also forward traces to Jaeger or X-Ray. We'll show a sample dashboard.
[08:47] Lina Ortega: If we use PrivateLink, how do we handle SSO and least privilege? We need RBAC on who can deploy models and who can alter routing.
[08:55] Alex Chen: We integrate with SAML/SCIM for SSO and support RBAC roles for deploy, read-only, and admin. Control-plane actions go over the management plane with mTLS and your authz rules. We can map SCIM groups to RBAC roles.
[09:07] Tej Patel: Any gotchas with EKS/ECS and node ports when using PrivateLink?
[09:13] Priya Raman: When using EKS, prefer using AWS VPC CNI with ENI trunking disabled for dense pods, ensure security groups allow traffic to the interface endpoints, and avoid hostPort unless necessary. For ECS Fargate, ensure task subnets have endpoints for image pulls and SSM if you need exec. We'll send a specific EKS/ECS checklist.
[09:33] Mark Voss: Let's discuss a failure scenario: if a PrivateLink endpoint goes down in an AZ, how does Redwood handle fallback?
[09:41] Priya Raman: Redwood supports fallback policies: you can route to another AZ's endpoint or fall back to a Redwood-managed public endpoint over secure path (if allowed). For strict air-gapped customers, you'd rely on cross-AZ endpoints and local caches. We also recommend client-side retry and circuit breaker patterns to avoid thundering herds.
[09:58] Tej Patel: For benchmarks — we want p50/p95/p99 across 1, 10, 100 concurrent users; can Redwood help run these within our staging VPC?
[10:08] Alex Chen: Yes. SE can run perf tests using our bench harness via a temporary PrivateLink endpoint and a staging subnet. We'll need a small footprint of runtime nodes and test scripts — Samir will coordinate.
[10:19] Samir Kapoor: I'll take lead on bench setup. We'll capture token-level breakdowns and include KV hit/miss rates so you can see real impact.
[10:26] Mark Voss: On the topic of quantization again — is model variant switching supported during rollouts? We want to test int8 vs fp16 in canary.
[10:34] Priya Raman: Yes, Redwood's rollout supports model variants and automatic fallback. You can do canary traffic split and measure latency/quality. Note quantized models sometimes show small quality regressions, we recommend evals across representative prompts.
[10:48] Lina Ortega: Do you have compliance artifacts for private deployment? We need SOC2, network diagrams, and an audit of k8s control plane hardening.
[10:56] Alex Chen: We'll share SOC2 and the network security appendix. For k8s hardening we document recommended pod security policies, RBAC and admission controls.
[11:07] Mark Voss: Great. Any other runtime optimizations specific to network topology?
[11:12] Priya Raman: A few bullets: minimize cross-VPC hops for KV cache; use per-AZ caches; prefer PrivateLink over public NAT for lower p99 variance; enable connection pooling and keepalives; pre-warm models or use quantized variants to reduce cold start; use network accelerated file systems or local disks for model weights to avoid cross-AZ pulls on scale-up.
[11:37] Tej Patel: For pre-warming, how do you recommend we size the pool? We don't want idle cost but want <100ms cold start.
[11:45] Samir Kapoor: Depends on your concurrency. We typically size a small baseline workers per AZ (based on historical qps) and autoscale with a short cooldown. Use predictive scaling if patterns are regular. We'll share an autoscale config template.
[11:58] Mark Voss: Ok good. Let's capture action items.
[12:02] Alex Chen: Quick recap and actions: we'll share network diagram, endpoint sizing guide, SOC2 docs, and bench plan. Samir to schedule bench. Customer to provision staging subnet and confirm IP allowlist.
[12:16] Mark Voss: Thanks team. Any final Qs?
[12:20] Lina Ortega: One more — can we limit which subnets can call the control plane? We don't want dev subnets with deploy rights.
[12:27] Alex Chen: Yes you can restrict management-plane access to specific subnets and use SGs plus RBAC — we enforce mTLS for control plane.
[12:33] Tej Patel: Perfect. We'll follow up with dates for the bench.
[12:36] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll send the docs. End.

Notes: transcription has occasional mislabels and small filler words preserved. References: /redwood/docs/private-vpc-networking (link), sample cost model spreadsheet (link: drive/references/aurelius-bench.xlsx).
